sections.h2: What do the Missouri guides by city and county cover?
sections.html:
This directory is the starting point for sellers across Missouri. It sits above 29 city selling pages, 5 city property tax guides, 41 county property tax guides, 18 recorder of deeds guides, and a set of statewide topic pages on tax appeals, homestead credits, evictions, deeds and capital gains.

The local pages answer questions that change at the county line: who bills the tax, where a deed is recorded, and which court handles a probate or eviction filing. This page covers what stays the same in all 114 counties and the City of St. Louis, which Missouri lists separately from any county.

sections.h2: How is Missouri laid out and where do homeowners live?
sections.html:
Missouri is a landlocked Midwestern state with about 6.27 million residents on the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate. The state holds 114 counties plus the independent City of St. Louis. Jefferson City is the capital, and the five largest cities are Kansas City, St. Louis, Springfield, Columbia and Independence, according to Wikipedia's Missouri entry.

The same entry names St. Louis County, Jackson County and St. Charles County as the three most populous counties, and Worth County as the least populated, with about 7 people per square mile. Texas County covers the most land. A house in Worth County and a house in St. Louis County sit under the same state statutes but meet very different markets, assessors and recorder offices.

sections.h2: How do Missouri's regions affect a house?
sections.html:
Terrain and weather differ a lot across the state. The Missouri River and Mississippi River frame much of the north and east, southern Missouri rises into the Ozarks, and the southeast corner is the Bootheel, described as the lowest, flattest, warmest and wettest part of the state.

  • Ozarks and karst. The southern plateau has limestone terrain with sinkholes and caves, so ask an inspector about ground movement on a house there.
  • Bootheel. Flat river-plain land in the Mississippi Alluvial Plain, with an economy that is mostly agricultural.
  • Tornado Alley. Missouri sits in an area of severe thunderstorms and tornadoes. The May 22, 2011 EF-5 tornado destroyed roughly a third of Joplin, so keep records of any storm repairs on a house you sell.

sections.h2: What is the history behind Missouri's county system?
sections.html: French fur traders founded Ste. Genevieve in 1735 and St. Louis in 1764, and the United States acquired the area in the Louisiana Purchase of 1803. Missouri was admitted as a state as part of the Missouri Compromise of 1820. After the Civil War, Greater St. Louis and the Kansas City area grew into major centers of industry and business.

The Census Bureau counts 2,508,227 households for 2020-2024, at 2.40 persons per household. Some other measures from the same table:

  • 87.4 percent of residents age one and over lived in the same house a year earlier.
  • 19.6 percent of residents are 65 or older, and 347,543 are veterans.
  • Mean travel time to work is 23.5 minutes.
  • The median selected monthly owner cost is $1,524 with a mortgage and $546 without one.

sections.h2: How does Missouri tax a home across all counties?
sections.html:
Each county assessor values residential property at nineteen percent of true value, under RSMo 137.115. Agricultural land is assessed at twelve percent and commercial property at thirty-two percent. The assessor sets new values in odd-numbered years, and those values carry into the following even-numbered year.

Tax relief runs through the Department of Revenue's Property Tax Credit Claim, with a maximum of $1,100 for owners and $750 for renters, and through a county credit for owners 62 and older under RSMo 137.1050 where a county has adopted it. The county collector, not the state, sends the bill, so the county page for your house is the one to open.

sections.h2: How does a Missouri foreclosure sale work?
sections.html:
Missouri foreclosures under a deed of trust are advertised in a newspaper, with the number of insertions depending on the county. RSMo 443.320 generally calls for at least twenty insertions in a daily newspaper in counties with a city of 50,000 or more, and four successive weekly issues in other counties. The notice must give the date and recording information of the deed of trust, the grantors, the time, terms and place of sale, and a description of the property.

Mail goes out as well. Under RSMo 443.325, the foreclosing party must deposit a certified or registered envelope in the mail at least twenty days before the sale, addressed to the record owner and to the borrower, and to anyone who recorded a request for notice at least forty days before the sale. Proof of mailing is enough, and the addressee does not have to sign for it.

sections.h2: How does a house pass out of a small Missouri estate?
sections.html:
A small estate can transfer without a full administration. RSMo 473.097 allows distributees to claim an estate without letters when everything left after liens and debts is worth no more than $40,000, thirty days have passed since the death, and no application for letters is pending.

  • The affiant files a sworn affidavit with the probate division that lists the property, the debts, and who receives each item.
  • A bond is filed unless the court finds it unnecessary, and the filing fee is paid.
  • When the listed property is over $15,000, the clerk publishes a notice to creditors once a week for two consecutive weeks.
  • The distributees show title to real estate by filing a copy of the affidavit and the clerk's certificate with the recorder of deeds in each county where the land lies.

Estates above the limit go through ordinary probate, and the county probate division can say which route fits.

sections.h2: How should a Missouri seller use these guides?
sections.html:
Start with the page for the county where the house stands, since the assessor, collector and recorder are county offices. Then read the topic page that matches the situation: a tenant in the house, a loan in default, an inherited house, or a tax bill that looks too high.

  • Pull the latest tax statement and compare the county's assessed value with recent sales.
  • Ask the recorder of deeds for the recorded deed and any liens before you set a price.
  • If a tenant lives there, note the lease type and any notice already given.
  • If the owner has died, find out whether the estate fits the small estate limit.

faqs.q: How many counties does Missouri have?
faqs.a: 114, plus the independent City of St. Louis, which is listed separately from St. Louis County. Wikipedia's Missouri page gives the count.

faqs.q: What is the median value of a Missouri home?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau puts the median value of owner-occupied housing units at $230,300 for 2020-2024, on its QuickFacts page for Missouri. County medians differ and are on each county guide.

faqs.q: What percentage of its value does Missouri assess a house at?
faqs.a: Nineteen percent for residential real property, according to RSMo 137.115. The assessor sets new values every odd-numbered year.

faqs.q: Does a Missouri foreclosure require notice to the owner?
faqs.a: Yes. RSMo 443.325 requires a certified or registered mailing at least twenty days before the sale to the record owner and the borrower, and RSMo 443.320 requires newspaper advertisement of the sale.

faqs.q: Can a Missouri house go through a small estate affidavit instead of probate?
faqs.a: Yes, when the estate after liens and debts is $40,000 or less and the other conditions of RSMo 473.097 are met. The distributee records the affidavit and clerk's certificate with the recorder of deeds to show title.
